reading: Volatility Smiles and the Fundamental Review of the Trading Book
setup: FRTB internal models. Five partial expected shortfalls on a 10-day base shock (EUR m): $ES_1, \dots, ES_5 = 40, 30, 20, 12, 6$, for liquidity horizons of 10, 20, 40, 60 and 120 days. Each $ES_j$ with $j \ge 2$ is scaled by $\sqrt{(LH_j - LH_{j-1})/10}$. The five scaled figures are then combined as the square root of the sum of their squares.
ask: Total expected shortfall is closest to:

options.label: ≈ EUR 19m
options.why: Scale slip (0.3×). The total can't be below $ES_1 = 40$ on its own, since every other term only adds under the square root.

options.label: ≈ EUR 170m
options.why: Scaled each category by its full horizon $\sqrt{LH_j/10}$ instead of the increment, then added the five figures in a straight line instead of in quadrature.

options.label: ≈ EUR 3,800m
options.why: Stopped at the sum of squares (3,804) and never took the square root.

takeaway: FRTB ES: scale by the horizon increment, then add in quadrature. The total lands above $ES_1$ but below the straight sum of the scaled partials (about 130).

reading: Volatility Smiles and the Fundamental Review of the Trading Book
setup: FRTB expected shortfall. Liquidity horizons are 10, 20, 40, 60 and 120 days. Each partial $ES_j$ ($j \ge 2$) is scaled by $\sqrt{(LH_j - LH_{j-1})/10}$ before aggregation. $ES_3$ belongs to the 40-day category and $ES_4$ to the 60-day category.
ask: Which scaling factor is larger: the one applied to $ES_3$ or the one applied to $ES_4$?

options.label: $ES_4$'s factor is larger
options.why: Scaled by the horizon level, $\sqrt{60/10} = 2.45$ against $\sqrt{40/10} = 2.00$. The formula uses the increment from the previous horizon, not the level.

options.label: $ES_3$'s factor is larger
options.why: This would need the 40→60 step to be shorter than the 20→40 step. Both increments are 20 days.

takeaway: FRTB horizon scaling uses the increment $LH_j - LH_{j-1}$, not the horizon itself. That makes categories 3 and 4 identical.

reading: Volatility Smiles and the Fundamental Review of the Trading Book
setup: Currency option parity: $p = c + Ke^{-rT} - S_0e^{-qT}$. The foreign rate acts as the yield $q$. Spot is USD 0.5500, strike USD 0.5700, $T = 1$. The domestic rate is $r = 4\%$ and the foreign rate is $q = 8\%$. The call trades at USD 0.0325, with an implied vol of 14.5%.
ask: The residual $Ke^{-rT} - S_0e^{-qT}$, which equals $p - c$, is:

options.label: Positive: the put is worth more than the call
Negative
options.why: Swapped the rates, discounting the strike at 8% and spot at 4%: $0.5262 - 0.5284 = -0.002$. The domestic rate discounts the domestic strike, and the foreign rate discounts spot.

options.label: Too close to call
options.why: The strike sits above spot and is also discounted at the lower rate. Both push $Ke^{-rT}$ above $S_0e^{-qT}$, and the gap is about 0.040, larger than the call price itself.

takeaway: In FX parity, $r$ (domestic) discounts the strike and $q$ (foreign) discounts spot. The implied vol is not needed.

reading: Volatility Smiles and the Fundamental Review of the Trading Book
setup: Using $\sigma = 34.0\%$, BSM values a European call at USD 6.95 and the matching European put (same strike and maturity) at USD 5.12. The call actually trades at USD 7.23.
ask: The put's market price is most likely:

options.label: Below USD 5.12
options.why: Flipped the sign of the error: $5.12 - 0.28 = 4.84$. The market pays more than BSM for the call, so it pays more for the put too.

options.label: Equal to USD 5.12
options.why: Put-call parity holds for both model and market prices, so any dollar mispricing BSM makes on the call it makes on the put.

takeaway: Same strike, same maturity: BSM's dollar pricing error is identical for the call and the put, and so is the implied vol.

reading: Volatility Smiles and the Fundamental Review of the Trading Book
setup: Bilinear interpolation on a volatility surface at $K/S_0 = 1.10$ and a maturity of 4.0 years. Interpolating across strike has already given 19.80% on the 2-year row and 21.60% on the 5-year row.
ask: The final 4-year implied volatility will be closer to:

options.label: 19.80% (the 2-year row)
options.why: Put the weight on the wrong end. The weight on the 5-year value is $(4-2)/(5-2) = 2/3$, because 4 years sits closer to 5 than to 2. Stopping at 19.80% is the other trap: that is the 2-year row, not the answer.

options.label: Exactly midway (20.70%)
options.why: The midpoint of 2 and 5 years is 3.5 years, not 4.

takeaway: Bilinear interpolation takes two passes, one in each dimension. Put each weight on the grid point the target is nearest to.

reading: Volatility Smiles and the Fundamental Review of the Trading Book
setup: Normal ES as a loss: $ES = -\mu + \sigma \times \frac{e^{-Y^2/2}}{\sqrt{2\pi}\,(1-X)}$. The daily mean return is $+1.0\%$, daily $\sigma = 5.0\%$, $X = 97.5\%$ and $Y = 1.96$. The tail term is already done: $5.0\% \times 2.338 = 11.69\%$.
ask: The daily 97.5% ES, expressed as a loss, is:

options.label: Above 11.69%
options.why: Added the mean, treating the +1% expected return as if it were an expected loss. An expected profit reduces the tail loss, so it is subtracted.

options.label: Exactly 11.69%
options.why: Dropped the $-\mu$ term. The mean is small, but it is stated and it moves the answer by a full percentage point.

takeaway: When the mean is an expected RETURN, subtract it from the tail term to get a loss.

reading: Volatility Smiles and the Fundamental Review of the Trading Book
setup: A USD 30m exposure is normally distributed. It is stated in loss-positive format: mean loss $+4.0\%$, $\sigma = 15.0\%$. The 97.5% ES multiplier is 2.3378, and the tail term is already done: $15.0\% \times 2.3378 = 35.07\%$.
ask: The 97.5% ES as a percentage of the exposure is:

options.label: Below 35.07%
options.why: Subtracted the mean as if it were an expected return. In loss-positive format, +4% is an expected loss, so it adds to the tail.

options.label: Exactly 35.07%
options.why: Dropped the mean term, which here is worth four percentage points.

takeaway: Read the format label first. A positive mean LOSS is added; a positive mean RETURN is subtracted.

reading: Volatility Smiles and the Fundamental Review of the Trading Book
setup: A USD 30m exposure is normally distributed. It is stated in loss-positive format: mean loss $4.0\%$, $\sigma = 15.0\%$. Use $ES_{97.5\%} = \mu + \sigma \times \phi(1.96)/(1 - 0.975)$, with $\phi(1.96) = 0.05845$.
ask: The single-period 97.5% ES is closest to:

options.label: ≈ USD 1.5m
options.why: Forgot to divide the density by the tail probability $(1 - X) = 0.025$. Without that, the multiplier is 0.058 when it should be 2.34.

options.label: ≈ USD 39m
options.why: Reported the percentage (39.1%) as the dollar figure and skipped the multiply by USD 30m. An ES above the whole exposure is an instant red flag.

options.label: ≈ USD 120m
options.why: Scale slip (10×). This is four times the exposure itself.

takeaway: The 97.5% normal ES is about $\mu + 2.34\sigma$, roughly 40% of this exposure. A figure above the whole position is a red flag.

reading: Tuckman, The Science of Term Structure Models
setup: Model 1 (normal, no drift): $dr = \sigma\,dw$. The current short rate is 7.18%, $\sigma = 118$ bp per year, and the step is three months ($dt = 0.25$). The realised draw is $dw = 0.18$.
ask: The change in the short rate over the step is closest to:

options.why: Also multiplied by $dt$. The realised $dw$ already carries the time scaling, because its s.d. is $\sqrt{dt}$, so $dt$ does not appear again.
Scale slip (10×). A 2% move in one quarter would be almost twice the whole annual volatility.
Plugged in 118 without converting basis points to percent: $118 \times 0.18 = 21.2$ is in basis points, not percent.

takeaway: Given a realised $dw$, the change is just $\sigma \times dw$. The time step only matters for the distribution of $dw$.

reading: Tuckman, The Science of Term Structure Models
setup: Model 2: $dr = \lambda\,dt + \sigma\,dw$, with $r_0 = 6.138\%$, $\lambda = 0.239\%$ per year and $\sigma = 1.20\%$ per year. The horizon is one month.
ask: The standard deviation of the one-month rate change is closest to:

options.why: Scaled $\sigma$ by $dt = 1/12$. That is the drift's scaling; dispersion scales with $\sqrt{dt}$.
Left $\sigma$ at its annual value, so the one-month horizon was never applied.
Multiplied by $\sqrt{12}$ instead of dividing. That stretches the annual figure outward when it should shrink it.

takeaway: Drift scales with $dt$ and dispersion with $\sqrt{dt}$, so write both side by side before substituting.

reading: Tuckman, The Science of Term Structure Models
setup: Model 2: $dr = \lambda\,dt + \sigma\,dw$, with $\lambda = 0.239\%$ per year and $\sigma = 1.20\%$ per year. The horizon is one month ($dt = 1/12$).
ask: Over the month, which is bigger: the expected drift $\lambda\,dt$ or the one-s.d. random move $\sigma\sqrt{dt}$?

options.label: The random move, by a wide margin
The drift
options.why: Compared the unscaled annual drift (0.239%) with $\sigma \times dt$ (0.10%). Each term needs its own time scaling.

options.label: They are about the same size
options.why: About 0.02% of drift against 0.35% of dispersion is a factor of roughly 17, not a match. Drift shrinks with $dt$, dispersion only with $\sqrt{dt}$.

takeaway: At short horizons dispersion swamps drift; drift only catches up at long horizons because $t$ outgrows $\sqrt{t}$.

reading: Tuckman, The Science of Term Structure Models
setup: Model 2: $dr = \lambda\,dt + \sigma\,dw$. The current rate is 5.26%, $\sigma = 115$ bp per year and $\lambda = 0.25\%$ per year. The step is one month, and the realised draw is $dw = 0.25$.
ask: The drift contribution $\lambda\,dt$ to this month's change is closest to:

options.label: ≈ 0.6 bp
options.why: Scale slip (0.3×).

options.label: ≈ 7.2 bp
options.why: Scaled the drift by $\sqrt{dt}$. That is the dispersion's scaling; drift is linear in $dt$.

options.label: ≈ 25 bp
options.why: Used the annual drift unscaled, which is the classic Model 2 slip.

takeaway: Over one month a 25 bp-a-year drift is only about 2 bp, small next to the random term.

reading: Tuckman, The Science of Term Structure Models
setup: Model 1 binomial tree with no drift. $r_0 = 4.00\%$, $\sigma = 1.20\%$ per year, and each step is three months ($dt = 0.25$). Each node moves up or down by $\sigma\sqrt{dt}$ with probability ½.
ask: Which is larger: the up-up node's distance above 4.00% after two steps, or one standard deviation of the six-month change, $\sigma\sqrt{2\,dt}$?

options.label: $\sigma\sqrt{2\,dt}$
options.why: Reversed the comparison. The extreme path is $2\sigma\sqrt{dt}$, which equals $\sqrt{2} \times \sigma\sqrt{2\,dt}$.

options.label: They are equal
options.why: Treated two steps as one step of length $2dt$. The tree's extreme path widens linearly in the number of steps, while the s.d. widens with its square root.

takeaway: A tree's outer nodes run $n\sigma\sqrt{dt}$ out, ahead of the $\sigma\sqrt{n\,dt}$ spread of the distribution.

reading: Tuckman, The Science of Term Structure Models
setup: Ho-Lee tree: $dr = \lambda(t)\,dt + \sigma\,dw$. $r_0 = 5.00\%$, $\sigma = 1.20\%$ per year, quarterly steps ($dt = 0.25$). The drift is $\lambda(1) = 0.40\%$ per year over step 1 and $\lambda(2) = 0.80\%$ per year over step 2.
ask: The middle node after two steps sits above 5.00% by roughly:

options.label: ≈ +0.03 pp
options.why: Scale slip (0.1×).

options.label: ≈ +0.10 pp
options.why: Applied only the first step's drift, $\lambda(1)\,dt$, and dropped the second.

options.label: ≈ +1.2 pp
options.why: Added the annual drifts unscaled ($0.40 + 0.80$) without multiplying each by $dt$.

takeaway: In a recombining tree, the up and down moves cancel on the middle path, so the middle node is just the start plus the sum of the dt-scaled drifts.

reading: Tuckman, The Science of Term Structure Models
setup: Model 3: $dr = \lambda(t)\,dt + \sigma e^{-\alpha t}\,dw$, with $\sigma = 1.50\%$ and $\alpha = 0.05$. At $t = 3$ years, $\lambda = 0.30\%$ per year, the step is one month and the realised $dw = 0.20$. With the undecayed $\sigma$ alone, $\sigma\,dw = 0.30\%$.
ask: After you add the drift and apply the volatility decay, the true $dr$ is:

options.label: Above 0.30%
options.why: Added the drift (+2.5 bp) but forgot that $e^{-0.15} = 0.861$ trims the random term by about 4.2 bp. That route gives 0.325%, reading $\sigma$ as constant.

options.label: Too close to call
options.why: The decay effect (−4.2 bp) is about 1.7× the drift (+2.5 bp), so the net is about −1.7 bp, clearly below.

takeaway: In Model 3, evaluate $\sigma e^{-\alpha t}$ first. By year 3 the decay costs more than a month of drift adds.

reading: Meissner, Correlation Risk
setup: A portfolio is LONG asset X and SHORT asset Y. Both assets have positive volatility and the position sizes are fixed. The correlation between X and Y rises.
ask: Variance-covariance portfolio VaR:

options.label: Rises
options.why: True when both positions are LONG. With one short, $w_1 w_2 < 0$, so the cross term $2w_1w_2\rho\sigma_1\sigma_2$ falls as $\rho$ rises.

options.label: Unchanged
options.why: Correlation enters through the cross term, which is non-zero whenever both positions are non-zero.

working.label: Sign of coefficient on $\rho$
working.display: $2 w_1 w_2 \sigma_1 \sigma_2 < 0$, so variance falls as $\rho$ rises

working.label: Result
working.display: Portfolio VaR falls; it is largest at $\rho = -1$

takeaway: Long-long: VaR rises with ρ. Long-short: the sign flips, and VaR peaks at ρ = −1.

reading: Meissner, Correlation Risk
setup: USD 10m is split 6:4 between asset X ($\sigma = 5\%$) and asset Y ($\sigma = 10\%$), $z = 2.33$. The two assets are currently perfectly correlated. The correlation then drops to zero.
ask: Portfolio VaR:

options.label: Rises
options.why: The two calculations were done correctly but the labels were swapped. For a long-only book, ρ = 1 is always the upper bound.

options.label: Unchanged
options.why: Correlation only drops out when one position is zero. Here both are live, so the cross term matters.

takeaway: For a long-only book, individual VaRs add at ρ = 1 and combine in quadrature at ρ = 0, so VaR falls as correlation falls.

reading: Meissner, Correlation Risk
setup: USD 10m is split 6:4 between asset X ($\sigma = 5\%$) and asset Y ($\sigma = 10\%$). The assets are uncorrelated. Use the variance-covariance approach with $z = 2.33$.
ask: Portfolio 99% VaR is closest to:

options.label: ≈ USD 0.10m
options.why: Used variances ($0.05^2$, $0.10^2$) in place of volatilities in the individual VaRs.

options.label: ≈ USD 12m
options.why: Scale slip (10×). That exceeds the entire USD 10m portfolio.

options.label: ≈ USD 120m
options.why: Entered volatilities as 5 and 10 instead of 0.05 and 0.10, a percent-vs-decimal slip that makes everything 100× too big.

takeaway: Uncorrelated VaRs combine in quadrature. Here that lands between the larger single VaR (0.93) and their sum (1.63).

reading: Meissner, Correlation Risk
setup: A USD 10m portfolio holds USD 3m in A (daily $\sigma_A = 3\%$) and USD 7m in B (daily $\sigma_B = 5\%$), with $\rho = 0.4$. Use the variance-covariance approach with $z = 2.33$.
ask: The one-day 99% portfolio VaR is closest to:

options.label: ≈ USD 0.036m
options.why: Multiplied the portfolio VARIANCE (0.00156) by value and $z$ without taking its square root.

options.label: ≈ USD 15m
options.why: Annualised by $\sqrt{250}$. The volatilities are daily and the question asks for one day.

options.label: ≈ USD 92m
options.why: Entered the weights as 30 and 70 instead of 0.3 and 0.7, which inflates the s.d. 100×.

takeaway: Sanity band: VaR must sit between the ρ = 0 figure (0.84) and the ρ = 1 figure (1.02).

reading: Dowd, Estimating Market Risk Measures: An Introduction and Overview
setup: There are 20 daily P&L observations (USD thousands). The ten worst are −84, −61, −47, −38, −30, −25, −19, −14, −9 and −5. At 90% confidence the tail holds $(1 - 0.90) \times 20 = 2$ observations, so the 90% VaR threshold is 61.
ask: The 90% expected shortfall is:

options.label: Exactly 61
options.why: Reported the threshold (the VaR) instead of averaging the losses inside the tail.

options.label: Below 61
options.why: ES averages losses at or beyond the VaR threshold, so it can't come in below VaR. To get below 61 you must have averaged observations from outside the tail.

takeaway: ES ≥ VaR at the same confidence level, always. If yours comes out lower, something is wrong.

reading: Dowd, Estimating Market Risk Measures: An Introduction and Overview
setup: The 95% ES is approximated as the plain average of five tail VaRs (EUR m): 18.0 at 96%, 20.5 at 97%, 24.0 at 98%, 30.0 at 99% and 42.5 at 99.9%.
ask: The resulting ES estimate is:

options.label: Equal to 24.0
options.why: Took the middle value of the list (the median). ES is a MEAN.

options.label: Below 24.0
options.why: The largest VaR sits 18.5 above 24.0 while the smallest is only 6.0 below. The skewed tail pulls the mean up, not down.

takeaway: ES averages the tail, so a long right tail drags it above the middle tail VaR.

reading: Dowd, Estimating Market Risk Measures: An Introduction and Overview
setup: You hold one share of a stock that closed yesterday at USD 100. The 95% historical-simulation VaR uses a 260-day window, so it reads off the $(1 - 0.95) \times 260 + 1 = 14$th worst return. Yesterday that return was −6.05% (VaR USD 6.05), and the 13th worst was −6.25%. Today the stock falls 10%, a new worst return, and a −3% day drops out of the window.
ask: Today's 95% VaR in USD, compared with yesterday's USD 6.05:

options.label: Rises
options.why: Updated only the quantile ($6.25\% \times 100 = 6.25$) and applied it to yesterday's price. The position is now worth USD 90.

options.label: Roughly unchanged
options.why: The two updates don't cancel. The quantile worsens by about 3%, the base falls by 10%, and the net change is about −7%.

working.label: New 14th-worst return
working.display: Every rank shifts down one, so the old 13th (−6.25%) becomes the new 14th

takeaway: A rolling HS VaR has two moving parts, the quantile AND the position value. A big loss can lower the dollar VaR.

reading: Dowd, Estimating Market Risk Measures: An Introduction and Overview
setup: The 95% historical-simulation VaR uses a 260-day window, so it reads off the 14th worst return. Yesterday the 13th and 14th worst were −6.25% and −6.05%. Today a −10% return enters the window, worse than every existing observation. The return leaving is −3%, which was not in the tail.
ask: Today's 14th-worst return, compared with −6.05%, is:

options.label: Better (a smaller loss)
options.why: Nothing leaves the tail. The departing −3% was never in the worst 16, so no rank moves up, and the new −10% pushes every rank down one.

options.label: The same
options.why: That would only hold if the new return were milder than −6.05%. At −10% it outranks all of them.

working.label: New rank of −10%
working.display: 1st worst; all others shift down one rank

takeaway: A new worst-ever return shifts every order statistic down one place, so the VaR quantile gets worse.

reading: Dowd, Estimating Market Risk Measures: An Introduction and Overview
setup: The standard error of a quantile (VaR) estimate is $se = \frac{1}{f(q)}\sqrt{p(1-p)/n}$, with $n = 1{,}000$. Moving from 95% to 99.9% confidence, $p(1-p)$ falls from 0.0475 to 0.000999, and the density at the quantile falls from 0.1031 to 0.00337.
ask: The net effect on the standard error is:

options.label: It falls
options.why: Looked only at $p(1-p)$, whose square-root ratio is about 0.145×, and forgot the density sits in the DENOMINATOR, where its ratio is about 30.6×.

options.label: Too close to call
options.why: The two effects are 0.145× and 30.6×. They net to about 4.4×, nowhere near a wash.

takeaway: Deep-tail VaR is estimated less precisely, because the density at the quantile collapses faster than $p(1-p)$ does.

reading: Dowd, Estimating Market Risk Measures: An Introduction and Overview
setup: Quantile standard error: $se = \frac{1}{f(q)}\sqrt{p(1-p)/n}$, with $n = 1{,}000$ in both cases. At 95%: $p(1-p) = 0.0475$ and $f(q) = 0.1031$. At 99.9%: $p(1-p) = 0.000999$ and $f(q) = 0.00337$.
ask: $se_{99.9\%} / se_{95\%}$ is closest to:

options.why: Took the raw ratio of $p(1-p)$ (0.000999 / 0.0475), with no square root and no density.
Took the square root of the $p(1-p)$ ratio but ignored the density, which is the bigger effect.
Used the density ratio (0.1031 / 0.00337) alone and dropped the offsetting $\sqrt{p(1-p)}$ term.

takeaway: The two effects multiply: roughly ×0.15 from $p(1-p)$ and ×31 from the density, so going deep into the tail costs precision.

reading: Meissner, Correlation Risk
setup: An exchange option pays $\max(S_1 - S_2, 0)$. The correlation between $S_1$ and $S_2$ rises, and each asset's own volatility is unchanged.
ask: The exchange option's value:

options.label: Rises
options.why: That is the BASKET call, which is an option on a sum. The exchange option is an option on a DIFFERENCE, where correlation enters with a minus sign.

options.label: Unchanged
options.why: Option value rises with the volatility of the underlying combination, and $\text{Var}(S_1 - S_2) = \sigma_1^2 + \sigma_2^2 - 2\rho\sigma_1\sigma_2$ moves with $\rho$.

working.label: Result
working.display: Less spread volatility, so the option is worth less

takeaway: An option on a difference loses value as correlation rises; an option on a sum gains value.

reading: Volatility Smiles and the Fundamental Review of the Trading Book
setup: Volatility follows a GARCH(1,1) process, and current volatility is ABOVE its long-run level.
ask: The term structure of volatility forecasts slopes:

options.label: Upward
options.why: That is the case when current volatility is BELOW long-run. GARCH itself imposes no upward slope.

options.label: Flat
options.why: Only if current volatility equals the long-run level. GARCH(1,1) mean-reverts, so forecasts drift toward the long-run level.

working.label: Mean reversion
working.display: Forecasts converge geometrically to the long-run variance

working.label: Result
working.display: Current > long-run, so forecasts decline with horizon: a downward slope

takeaway: GARCH term structure: the slope points from the current volatility toward the long-run level.

reading: Volatility Smiles and the Fundamental Review of the Trading Book
setup: FX rates violate both lognormality conditions: their volatility is non-constant and they jump. The result is a pronounced FX volatility smile.
ask: As option maturity increases, the implied-volatility smile becomes:

options.label: More pronounced
options.why: Non-constant volatility makes the effect on PRICES more pronounced with maturity. The smile plots IMPLIED volatilities, and there both channels weaken.

options.label: No different
options.why: The jump effect on implied volatility fades with maturity. Short-dated rows of a surface are visibly more curved than long-dated ones.

working.label: Non-constant vol, effect on implied vol

takeaway: Smiles are sharpest at short maturities; both FX channels fade in implied-volatility terms as T grows.

reading: Volatility Smiles and the Fundamental Review of the Trading Book
setup: A firm's debt load is roughly fixed. Its equity value falls.
ask: Under the capital-structure leverage argument, the equity's volatility:

options.label: Falls
options.why: Reverses the leverage effect. Lower equity against fixed debt raises the debt-to-equity ratio and amplifies swings on the residual equity claim.

options.label: Unchanged
options.why: That holds only with zero debt, where equity volatility equals EBIT volatility.

working.label: Debt-to-equity
working.display: Equity down with debt fixed, so D/E rises

working.label: Result
working.display: Higher leverage amplifies equity volatility, so price down means volatility up

takeaway: Falling equity raises leverage and so volatility. That negative price–vol link is one reason for the downward equity skew.

reading: Volatility Smiles and the Fundamental Review of the Trading Book
setup: The FRTB switched from 99% VaR to 97.5% ES. Under normality, 99% VaR $= \mu + 2.326\sigma$ and 97.5% ES $= \mu + 2.338\sigma$, which are nearly equal. Now suppose losses have a heavier tail than the normal.
ask: Compared with the 99% VaR, the 97.5% ES is:

options.label: Smaller
options.why: Focused on the lower confidence level. ES averages the whole tail beyond its quantile, so a heavy tail raises it more than it raises a single quantile.

options.label: Roughly equal
options.why: Near-equality is the normal-distribution result. Heavy tails break it.

working.label: Heavy tail
working.display: VaR ignores the shape beyond the quantile; ES averages it

working.label: Result
working.display: 97.5% ES exceeds 99% VaR, possibly by a lot

takeaway: The switch is capital-neutral only under normality. Heavy tails make 97.5% ES bite harder than 99% VaR.

reading: Dowd, Estimating Market Risk Measures: An Introduction and Overview
setup: In volatility-weighted historical simulation, one month ago the asset returned 5%. The daily volatility estimate at that time was 2%, and today's daily volatility forecast is 1.5%.
ask: The volatility-adjusted return, compared with 5%, is:

options.label: Larger
options.why: Inverted the ratio: $5\% \times 2/1.5 = 6.67\%$. Current volatility goes on top.

options.label: The same
options.why: That is basic HS. Volatility weighting rescales by $\sigma_{\text{now}}/\sigma_{\text{then}} = 0.75$.

takeaway: Calmer now than then means old returns get scaled DOWN. Current volatility goes in the numerator.

reading: Dowd, Estimating Market Risk Measures: An Introduction and Overview
setup: A USD 1m equity portfolio, one-year horizon: mean 15%, volatility 25%, $z = 2.33$. Under normal returns, 99% VaR $= (-0.15 + 0.25 \times 2.33) \times 1\text{m} = \text{USD } 432{,}500$. You switch to lognormal: $VaR = P\,[1 - \exp(\mu - \sigma z)]$.
ask: The lognormal VaR, compared with USD 432,500, is:

options.label: Higher
options.why: Since $e^{-x} > 1 - x$, the lognormal loss $1 - e^{-0.4325}$ is always below the normal $0.4325$. Lognormal also caps the loss at the full value.

options.label: The same
options.why: The exponent equals the normal bracket, $-0.4325$, but $1 - e^{-0.4325} = 0.351$, not 0.4325.

takeaway: For the same μ and σ, lognormal VaR is always below normal VaR, because $1 - e^{-x} < x$.

reading: Dowd, Estimating Market Risk Measures: An Introduction and Overview
setup: Stock A's past 260 daily returns are highly NEGATIVELY skewed. P1 is long stock A; P2 is the same-size short position.
ask: Moving from P1 (long) to P2 (short), the absolute 99% VaR:

options.label: Rises
options.why: That is the positive-skew case. With negative skew the long LEFT tail hurts the long position, not the short.

options.label: Unchanged

reading: Hull, Ch. 20: Volatility Smiles
setup: An at-the-money call has strike USD 20.00 and BSM delta 0.50. The implied distribution has a LIGHT left tail and a HEAVY right tail, so implied volatility rises with $K/S_0$. The stock now rises toward USD 21.00.
ask: The call's TRUE delta:

options.label: Rises above 0.50
options.why: Counted only the BSM term ($N(d_1)$ rises). The smile term, vega × $\partial\sigma_{imp}/\partial S$, is negative here.

options.label: Falls below 0.50
options.why: Counted only the smile term. The standard BSM term pushes delta up.

options.label: Stays at 0.50
options.why: Ignores both terms; neither is zero here.

working.label: Term 1: BSM
working.display: $\partial c/\partial S$ rises as the option moves into the money: positive

working.label: Term 2: smile
working.display: $S$ up means $K/S_0$ down, so $\sigma_{imp}$ falls; vega > 0, so the term is negative

working.label: Net
working.display: The two terms oppose, so the direction is indeterminate

takeaway: True delta = BSM delta + vega × ∂σ/∂S. Under a reverse skew the two terms fight, so you need magnitudes.

reading: Empirical Approaches to Risk Metrics and Hedging
setup: You are hedging USD 100m face of a bond (DV01 0.300) with an instrument whose DV01 is 0.250. The DV01-neutral hedge is USD 120m face, short. A regression of the bond's yield changes on the hedge's yield changes gives beta = 0.800.
ask: The regression hedge's face value, compared with USD 120m, is:

options.label: Larger
options.why: Divided by beta ($120 / 0.8 = 150$) instead of multiplying.

options.label: The same
options.why: Beta scales the DV01-neutral size, and only β = 1 leaves it unchanged.

takeaway: If beta < 1, the regression hedge is smaller than the DV01-neutral hedge.
